paragraphs: The laws are inflexible and cannot adapt themselves to circumstances. In certain cases this may make them disastrous, and at a time of crisis cause the ruin of the State. The order and slowness of the forms they prescribe require a stretch of time that circumstances sometimes refuse. A thousand cases may arise for which the legislator has made no provision, and part of being foresighted, and a very necessary part, is to know that everything cannot be foreseen.
It is wrong, therefore, to want political institutions so strong that it becomes impossible to suspend their operation. Even Sparta let its laws lapse.

However, only the greatest dangers can outweigh the danger of changing the public order, and the sacred power of the laws should never be halted except when the existence of the country is at stake. In these rare and obvious cases, the public security is provided for by a special act that entrusts it to the person most worthy. This entrusting can be carried out in either of two ways, depending on the nature of the danger.

If making the government more active is a sufficient remedy, power is concentrated in the hands of one or two of its members. In that case it is not the authority of the laws that changes, but only the form of administering them. If, on the other hand, the peril is of such a kind that the apparatus of the laws is an obstacle to preserving them, the method is to name a supreme ruler who silences all the laws and, for a moment, suspends the sovereign authority. In such a case there is no doubt about the general will, and it is clear that the people’s first intention is that the State shall not perish. So the suspension of the legislative authority is in no sense its abolition. The magistrate who silences it cannot make it speak; he dominates it, but cannot represent it. He can do anything except make laws.

The Roman senate used the first method when, in a consecrated formula, it charged the consuls to provide for the safety of the Republic. The second was used when one of the two consuls named a dictator,[1] a custom Rome borrowed from Alba.

In the first period of the Republic, the dictatorship was very often used, because the State did not yet have a firm enough basis to maintain itself by the strength of its constitution alone. The state of morals at that time made many precautions unnecessary that would have been needed at other times. There was no fear that a dictator would abuse his authority or try to keep it beyond his term of office. On the contrary, so much power seemed to weigh on the man who held it, and he made all speed to lay it down, as if taking the place of the laws were too troublesome and too perilous a position to keep.

It is therefore not the danger of abuse but the danger of cheapening that makes me object to the careless use of this supreme magistracy in the earliest times. As long as it was freely used at elections, dedications and purely formal functions, there was a danger that it would become less formidable in time of need, and that men would grow used to regarding as empty a title that was used only on occasions of empty ceremony.

Toward the end of the Republic, the Romans, having grown more cautious, were as unreasonably sparing in their use of the dictatorship as they had earlier been lavish. It is easy to see that their fears were groundless: the weakness of the capital protected it against the magistrates who were in its midst; a dictator might in certain cases defend public liberty, but could never endanger it; and the chains of Rome would be forged not in Rome itself but in her armies. The weak resistance Marius offered to Sulla, and Pompey to Caesar, clearly showed what could be expected from authority at home against force from abroad.

This misconception led the Romans into great mistakes, such as the failure to name a dictator during the Catilinarian conspiracy. Only the city itself, with at most some province of Italy, was concerned, so the unlimited authority the laws gave a dictator would have let him make short work of the conspiracy. In fact it was put down only by a combination of lucky chances that human prudence had no right to expect.

Instead, the senate was content to entrust its whole power to the consuls. As a result Cicero, in order to act effectively, was forced to exceed his powers on a capital point. In the first transports of joy his conduct was approved, but later he was justly called to account for the blood of citizens shed in violation of the laws. Such a reproach could never have been made against a dictator. But the consul’s eloquence carried the day, and he himself, Roman though he was, loved his own glory better than his country. He sought not so much the most lawful and secure means of saving the State as to win for himself the whole honor of having done so.[2] He was therefore justly honored as the liberator of Rome, and also justly punished as a lawbreaker. However brilliant his recall may have been, it was undoubtedly an act of pardon.

However this important trust is conferred, its duration should be fixed at a very brief period that can never be prolonged. In the crises that lead to it, the State is either soon lost or soon saved, and once the present need has passed, the dictatorship becomes either tyrannical or idle. At Rome dictators held office for six months only, and most of them stepped down before their time was up. Had their term been longer, they might well have tried to prolong it still further, as the decemvirs did when they were chosen for a year. The dictator had only enough time to provide against the need that had caused him to be chosen; he had none to think of further projects.
